blocks.label: Education first
blocks.heading: AI and teaching this month
blocks.deck: Four stories for faculty, each with a suggestion for your classroom.

blocks.html: Access labels: UM access means UM subscribes, so sign in with your UM account (The Chronicle of Higher Education, The New York Times). Free needs no login. Metered allows a few free articles a month.

blocks.head: Faculty are watching students more closely. Is it worth the cost?
blocks.body: Beth McMurtrie reports that professors now monitor students through AI detectors, keystroke and draft logs, webcams and lockdown browsers, or move writing and tests back into the classroom. She finds that these measures strain trust, take up faculty time and may weaken the independent thinking college is meant to build. Some campuses are trying tech-free study and writing spaces instead.
blocks.classroom: Before adding a monitoring tool, ask what it tells you that a conversation with the student would not. The Academic Integrity Icons tool below is one way to set expectations up front instead.

blocks.head: Schools are adopting AI faster than anyone can measure whether it helps
blocks.body: An NPR series by Lee V. Gaines follows K-12 districts that are piloting AI for lesson planning, progress tracking and chatbot feedback, including an emotional-support chatbot at an Ohio alternative school. Research on student outcomes is thin, there is no agreed way to measure success, and most states have issued no guidance. These are the habits our incoming students will bring with them.

links.title: Schools are experimenting with AI with little evidence or policy to guide them
Schools struggle to measure how much AI experiments are helping

blocks.classroom: Ask students in the first week how AI was used in their high school classes and what rules they were given.

blocks.head: Do faculty play by the rules they set for students?
blocks.body: Several Chronicle pieces this month turn the AI question toward faculty. A journal asked political scientist Allison Stanger to resubmit an accepted article because some sentences seemed AI-written, and she argues that scholarly writing should be judged on substance. Dan Sarofian-Butin reviewed 1,191 education-leadership dissertations from 2025 and reports that about a third contained substantial AI-generated text. A College Matters episode asks whether administrators who use AI in their writing should disclose it.

links.title: Who Cares Whether Academics Use AI to Write?
Has AI Destroyed the Doctoral Dissertation?
The AI Police Are Coming for Everybody (podcast)

blocks.classroom: If you advise graduate students or serve on committees, talk with your program about what AI disclosure should look like in theses and dissertations.

blocks.head: Two classroom moves you can try this semester
blocks.body: At the University of Nevada, Reno, Sean O'Neil replaced some written work with graded discussions, using practice rounds and small 'spotlight' groups to prepare students. Separately, Sam Wineburg and Nadav Ziv found that about three in ten high schoolers trusted a false chatbot answer and none checked it, and they suggest simple habits such as asking follow-up questions and comparing answers to the same prompt.

links.title: Using Graded Discussions to Reduce AI Abuse and Build Skills
Think Your Students Know More About AI Than You Do? Read This

blocks.classroom: Try one class period where students check a chatbot answer against two sources before discussing it.

blocks.label: Student voices
blocks.heading: Students on how AI is changing their work
blocks.deck: Stories where students describe how AI is changing their own work. Both are from earlier this fall; we will keep looking for new ones each month.

blocks.title: Student Journalists: AI Is Changing Our Work, and Not For the Better
blocks.html: Three high school journalists describe AI straining trust between writers and editors, unreliable detectors, and teachers who use chatbots to plan and grade while asking students not to.

blocks.title: Student Artists Wrestle with AI's Promise and Peril
blocks.html: Young winners of a Boston art competition made work about AI in their communities, and several chose to limit or avoid AI in their own pieces.

blocks.head: Regulators move against chatbot makers over harm to young users
blocks.body: A Common Sense Media test found that most of the safeguards in ChatGPT for Teens did not work, and the chatbot rarely alerted parents when conversations turned to self-harm. Days later, eight states sued OpenAI under consumer-protection law, and Character.AI, the companion-chatbot company tied to teen-suicide lawsuits, filed for bankruptcy. Many students turn to chatbots for emotional support, so this matters for advising as well.

links.title: ChatGPT for Teens has special safeguards. A watchdog group finds most don't work
OpenAI sued by 8 states over ChatGPT safety concerns

blocks.head: Platforms and prizes try to separate human work from machine work
blocks.body: Deezer will let listeners hide fully AI-generated music, which now makes up more than half of its daily uploads. Comedians report AI avatars on Instagram copying their routines nearly word for word. A Quebec novelist lost a Goncourt nomination after an AI detector flagged his book, which he says he wrote himself. The detector problem is the same one faculty face with student writing.

links.title: Deezer will soon let you filter out AI-generated music
Canadian publisher supports Quebec novelist after AI denial

blocks.head: Entry-level work shrinks while colleges add AI programs
blocks.body: Anthropic reported that junior technical hires fell from 27% to 9% of its technical hiring. NPR's The Indicator looks at colleges launching applied-AI majors as humanities degrees decline, and Inside Higher Ed reports that philosophy departments are hiring AI specialists even as the wider humanities job market shrinks.

links.title: New career paths: Colleges now offer degrees in influencing and AI
Universities Are on an AI Philosopher Hiring Spree
Anthropic says its workforce has become less junior

blocks.label: Made at UM
blocks.heading: Two UM resources to try this month

blocks.label: Made at UM · For students, any discipline
blocks.heading: Pause Before You Prompt
blocks.html: A short reflection students complete before deciding whether to use AI on a task. It is built on a framework by Maggie Boyd and colleagues at Boston University (2025). Seven questions are arranged as petals: personal motives, accuracy, ethics, consequences, privacy, copyright and transparency. The aim is to keep students in charge of their own learning instead of treating AI as a co-writer.

blocks.alt: Opening screen of the Pause Before You Prompt interactive, with a pause button at the center of a flower of seven petals.
blocks.caption: The digital version opens on the seven petals. Students choose two or three to work through.

blocks.title: Analog version
blocks.html: A handout for class discussion or written reflection. Students start from each petal's question and branch into sub-questions. Instructor notes suggest scaffolding it over time and pairing it with recent news on AI's effects.

blocks.title: Digital version
blocks.html: An interactive for online and hybrid courses. Students pick two or three petals, read from 16 linked critical sources, write a reflection for each and a final decision, then export it as a web page or PDF to submit. Responses stay in the student's browser.
Try it: Assign it before the first assignment where AI use is permitted, and collect the export.

blocks.label: Made at UM · For faculty, shared with students
blocks.heading: Academic Integrity Icons
blocks.html: A builder that shows students, at a glance, what they may and may not do on an assignment. You choose a rule in up to ten categories, including getting help, collaboration, reuse of prior work, open-book research, where the work is done, citation, devices and late work. The AI category uses the five levels of the AI Assessment Scale (Perkins, Furze, Roe and MacVaugh), from No AI to AI Exploration. Each rule shows as a badge marked Permitted, Conditions apply or Not permitted.

blocks.alt: The Academic Integrity Icons builder: category cards with option buttons on the left and a live Assignment Guidelines preview on the right, with each rule marked Not permitted.
blocks.caption: The builder set up for an in-class exam. Pick options on the left; the badge set students will see updates on the right.

items: Pick one option per category and switch off any category that does not apply. The preview updates as you go.
Name the assignment, for example Essay 2: Rhetorical Analysis.
Open Share & embed and choose a student link, an embed for a Blackboard page, paste-in HTML that works in Blackboard, email or Word, or a SCORM package. Badges also download as PNG or SVG.
The settings live in the link, so bookmark it to reuse or adjust the set later.
In-class exam: No outside help, individual work, no reuse, closed book, in class or proctored, AI Level 1 (No AI).
Take-home essay: Writing center help allowed, discuss ideas but submit your own work, cite your own prior work, open research, take-home, AI Level 3 (AI Collaboration).

blocks.html: Try it: Paste the badge set at the top of each assignment in Blackboard so the rules sit next to the instructions.

blocks.label: Open call · No deadline
blocks.heading: Bring an idea. Leave with a working prototype.
blocks.html: The Grove Lab is AIG's tinkering lab for faculty who want to see what agentic AI can build for their teaching or research. You bring the idea and the subject expertise. AIG uses an agentic harness to build a working browser-based prototype with you, then you try it, react to it and decide what happens next. Submit a build idea · Browse the gallery · Read the guidelines · Questions: mwatkins@olemiss.edu

items: You describe it. A few plain sentences about what students or researchers should be able to do.
The agent builds it. Directed by AIG, an AI agent plans the app, writes the code and tests it in a browser.
You try it. You use the prototype, react and ask for changes. A prototype is for trying and discussing.
You decide. Keep it private, show it at an AI Institute or Task Force meeting, or share it in the gallery with credit.

blocks.label: What you get
blocks.html:
• A conversation about whether current agentic tools fit your idea
• A working prototype that runs in any browser, aligned with your learning or research goals
• A gallery of about 35 earlier builds to borrow ideas from
• A chance to show your build at an AI Institute or Task Force meeting, with credit

blocks.label: Know the limits
blocks.html:
• Prototypes only. Each needs review for accessibility, security and student data before students use it
• No student data: no names, ID numbers, grades or work tied to a person
• Most builds take a week or more, and AIG cannot take every request
• Accounts, servers, live AI or student records need a conversation first
• No gambling or prediction markets, deepfakes, assignment traps or spam-like bots

blocks.text: Two builds that show what an agent can do

blocks.label: Research and outside data
blocks.heading: A Living Century of Antibiotics
blocks.html:
What it does. An interactive history of antibiotic discovery joined to real resistance surveillance. Students drag a timeline from 1928 to 2026 to see when each drug arrived and when resistance was first documented. In the Live Data Lab they choose a bacterium, antibiotic, country, specimen and year and watch a dish of colonies respond in proportion to the reported share of resistant isolates. A Compare view sets two drugs side by side and says so when the numbers come from different organisms or methods.

What the agent built. Connected the app to five public sources: the WHO Global Health Observatory, CDC BEAM, ClinicalTrials.gov, PubMed and openFDA. Added an evidence inspector so every number on screen traces back to its source. AI drafted the historical narratives from cited sources; the surveillance figures come straight from the data and are never generated.

Fits courses in: Biology, microbiology, nursing, pharmacy, public health, history of science. Grove Lab scale: Involved (live outside data).
Try it in class: Have students find a drug and bacterium pair where resistance rose, trace the figure on the Sources page, and explain what a percentage of tested isolates does and does not tell a patient.
Built by Marc Watkins with Claude. Interaction concept adapted from A Century of Antibiotics by Soumya. Open the build

blocks.alt: Opening screen of A Living Century of Antibiotics: a dark petri dish with drifting bacteria and the headline A living century of antibiotics.
blocks.caption: Live Data Lab: pick a bacterium, drug, place and year, then apply the antibiotic.

blocks.label: Stand-alone learning app
blocks.heading: Write Music: The Sentence Sound Lab
blocks.html:
What it does. Turns Gary Provost's lesson on sentence variety into something students can see and hear. Each sentence is colored by length on a heat map, from a one-to-three-word Spark to a Crescendo of 25 words or more, and the text plays as music, with each word a note and each sentence break a rest. Students read 18 public-domain writers in the Library, paste in their own draft, shape the sound in the Studio, record themselves reading in the Booth, then reflect and export.

What the agent built. Built the whole lab as a single web page: the heat map, a synthesizer that runs on the browser's own audio engine, a recording booth, reflection prompts, exports (HTML report, PDF and WAV audio) and a 12-page printable packet for screen-free practice. There are no accounts and no server, and student writing stays in the student's browser.

Fits courses in: Composition, creative writing, journalism, speech, English language learners. Grove Lab scale: Moderate (several screens, saved work, export).
Try it in class: Students paste a paragraph from a current draft, find one run of same-length sentences, revise it, and export the before-and-after report with a short reflection.
Built by Marc Watkins with Claude, based on Gary Provost's 100 Ways to Improve Your Writing (1985). Open the build

blocks.alt: Opening screen of Write Music: the headline Hear What Your Sentences Are Playing beside a paragraph with each sentence highlighted in a color for its length.
blocks.caption: A monotone sample: six sentences of six words. Variety score 0/100.

blocks.html: Ready to try? Describe your idea in a few sentences on the build form, download it, and email it to mwatkins@olemiss.edu with the subject line Grove Lab build idea.

blocks.label: Disclosure
blocks.heading: How this issue was made

items.text: Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, used in Claude's Cowork mode.

Searched for news, giving priority to NPR, The Chronicle of Higher Education and The New York Times and to education stories. Opened each article to confirm its date, outlet and access. Drafted the summaries and classroom suggestions, gathered events, calls and resources from their own pages, wrote the Made at UM and Grove Lab descriptions from those tools' public pages, captured the tool screenshots in the web edition by running each tool's public code, and laid out the page, the Google Doc and the email edition.

Marc Watkins set the scope, priorities and sources, chose the Made at UM tools and the Grove Lab call, and reviews and edits each issue before it is sent. He writes the editor's note. This pilot issue has not yet been reviewed.

AI summaries can get details wrong, so read the original before citing. NPR and The New York Times block automated reading, so NPR stories were checked on member-station copies, and no Times stories on these topics were found for this period. Event details can change.
No AI-generated images. Grove Lab images come from the lab's own gallery. No student or personnel data.
